summary: Mexico lost more than 500,000 industrial jobs in June, with services also shedding workers despite the World Cup, deepening signs of a weakening labor market. The United States reopened its border to Mexican cattle imports after a year-long screwworm-related suspension that had pushed up US beef prices. Mexican and US officials finished a third round of talks reviewing the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement, agreeing to meet again in Washington in September. Separately, Mexico has recorded 14 mayors killed since Sheinbaum took office.

lead.h1: Mexico loses more than 500,000 industrial jobs in June
lead.context: The services sector also reported sharp job losses despite the World Cup, adding to signs of a weakening labor market this year.
lead.background: Mexico's National Occupation and Employment Survey (national labor survey), run by Mexico's statistics agency, tracks month-to-month changes in formal and informal employment across sectors including manufacturing, construction, mining and services.
lead.view: A monthly drop of 611,978 industrial jobs, with manufacturing accounting for 482,652 of that and construction another 120,877, is a sharp reversal for an economy already growing near 0.6% in 2025 with fixed investment falling from 23.8% to 22.4% of gross domestic product. The construction losses matter most for nearshoring claims, because physical construction, not investment announcements, is the actual evidence that new plants are being built. Services losing 597,891 jobs the same month, despite World Cup-driven demand, suggests the weakness is broad rather than sector-specific.
lead.prediction: Further national labor survey readings are likely to show continued softness in manufacturing and construction employment unless fixed investment as a share of gross domestic product stops declining. That view would be wrong if the next national labor survey release shows industrial employment rebounding without a matching jump in fixed investment or grid connections.

items.headline: United States reopens border to Mexican cattle imports after year-long ban
items.context: The US had blocked Mexican cattle for more than a year to contain rising beef prices for American consumers. The reopening is meant to ease pressure on meat costs while keeping monitoring in place.
items.background: The United States suspended Mexican cattle imports for more than a year after detecting New World screwworm, a parasite that can kill cattle within days, and the ban became entangled with a separate US effort to bring down record domestic beef prices.
items.view: Reopening one port of entry, with two more to follow later, is a phased and partial move, not a full resumption of pre-ban trade. The immediate winners are Mexican cattle exporters near Douglas, Arizona, and US buyers facing high beef prices, but continued screwworm monitoring means the reopening depends on the parasite staying under control rather than on the trade relationship alone.
items.prediction: Cattle shipments through Douglas most likely resume on the stated 30-day timeline, with the New Mexico ports following afterward. That would be wrong if a new screwworm detection forces the US to suspend the reopening before shipments start.

items.headline: US reopens border to Mexican cattle imports after screwworm-related suspension
items.context: The reopening lets Mexico resume live cattle exports to the US after two suspension periods tied to a screwworm outbreak had cut shipments and pushed up US beef prices.
items.background: Mexico suspended live cattle shipments to the United States twice after a screwworm outbreak, a parasite that infests livestock and can spread quickly once it crosses the border.
items.view: The reopening restores a trade channel that had been shut for animal health reasons rather than economic ones, so ranchers regain access to the US market they had before the outbreak. The arrangement now depends on Mexico controlling the parasite, not on any shift in US demand for beef.
items.prediction: Cattle shipments are likely to resume and continue without interruption. That would be proven wrong if new screwworm cases are detected and the United States closes the border again.

items.headline: Third round of trade agreement review ends with plans for September meeting
items.context: Mexican and US officials completed a third round of technical talks on the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement and agreed to reconvene in Washington in September, part of the pact's first mandated joint review.
items.background: Under Article 34.7 of the trade agreement, the United States, Mexico and Canada must hold a joint review since Washington declined the option of a 16-year extension on 1 July 2026, and the countries now review the pact annually rather than renegotiating it outright.
items.view: A third round ending in another meeting date, rather than a text or a decision, shows the review is still at the technical-talks stage, not the negotiating stage. Steel, aluminum and Chinese-content rules are being discussed, but nothing here changes rules of origin or tariffs for a single exporter yet. The benefit for now goes to officials who can point to "constructive" progress without committing either government to a position.
items.prediction: The fourth round in September most likely produces further technical alignment rather than a signed change to the agreement's terms. That expectation would be wrong if the September meeting instead produces a joint statement on specific rule changes, such as new steel or automotive content thresholds.
items.drivers: Talks focused on steel, aluminum and derivative products, regional value chains, and reducing reliance on Asian imports, led by Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard and US trade office Jamieson Greer.
items.next: The two governments will hold a fourth round of talks in the first half of September to continue the joint review.

items.headline: Mexico records 14 mayors killed since Sheinbaum took office
items.context: The tally underscores the risk facing local officials and the limits of federal security strategy in territories where organized crime groups compete for local political control.
items.background: Oaxaca and Michoacan have recorded the most mayoral killings among Mexican states over the past 18 months, according to the tally cited in reporting.
items.view: Fourteen mayors killed since October 2024 already exceeds the total recorded over some full past presidential terms, according to the cited count, indicating the pace of killings has accelerated rather than held steady. The yearly totals cited, three in 2024, eight in 2025 and three so far in 2026, show the toll is not concentrated in a single spike.
items.prediction: Killings of local officials are likely to continue at a similar pace without a targeted change in strategy toward municipal capture. That would be disproven if the annual count drops well below the 2025 pace.
